name: Pueblo Blue Corn Atole
imageAlt: Blue cornmeal used for Pueblo-style atole
imageCredit: Illustrative blue-corn image via Wikimedia Commons; not a verified finished-dish photograph.
summary: A Pueblo-focused blue corn atole home adaptation: toasted blue cornmeal whisked into water until smooth, warm and lightly nutty.
lead: Blue cornmeal is toasted first, then whisked slowly into water for a warm, sustaining drink-porridge.
about: Blue corn atole appears in Southwestern Indigenous and Pueblo food contexts as a simple preparation of finely ground corn cooked with water. Texture can range from drinkable to spoon-thick. This version stays deliberately plain and uses no ceremonial claims.
story: Blue corn carries specific agricultural and cultural significance across Pueblo communities. Public educational materials document blue-corn porridges and drinks, but household and community methods vary, so this page is framed as a home adaptation rather than a definitive traditional recipe.
caveat: This is a general home adaptation based on public Pueblo foodway documentation, not a ceremonial formula.
prepNotes: Atole may be drinkable or spoonable.
ingredients: 1 tbsp maple syrup or honey, optional
steps: Toast cornmeal in a dry saucepan over medium-low heat 3–4 minutes.
Whisk toasted meal with 1 cup cool water until smooth.
Add remaining water gradually while whisking.
Bring to a gentle simmer and cook 12–15 minutes.
Checkpoint: mixture should be fully smooth with no raw gritty taste.
Thin with hot water if desired and season with salt.
Add optional sweetener only at the table.
sources: Indian Pueblo Cultural Center — Pueblo foodways

name: Sudanese Gurasa
imageCredit: Illustrative flatbread image via Wikimedia Commons; not a verified finished gurasa photograph.
summary: Sudanese gurasa: soft, lightly fermented wheat flatbreads cooked on a griddle and used to scoop stews and sauces.
lead: A loose yeast dough cooks into soft, flexible rounds designed to absorb the sauces of a Sudanese meal.
about: Gurasa is a Sudanese wheat flatbread that can range from pancake-like to thicker griddle bread depending on household and region. It is commonly eaten with stews, beans and meat sauces and should remain soft enough to tear and scoop.
story: Alongside kisra, gurasa is part of Sudan's diverse bread traditions. Wheat-based gurasa is especially practical in home kitchens without the specialized surfaces used for some traditional breads.
caveat: Thickness and fermentation vary widely; this version uses a short yeast fermentation and skillet cooking.
steps: Whisk flour, yeast and salt.
Add warm water to make a thick pourable batter-dough.
Cover and rest 35–45 minutes until visibly bubbly.
Lightly oil a skillet and pour about 1/2 cup batter, spreading into a round.
Cook until the surface loses its wet shine, then flip briefly.
Checkpoint: bread should be cooked through but still flexible and pale-golden rather than crisp.
Stack under a towel and serve warm.
sources: Fringe Table — Horn & Northeast Africa guide

name: Nigerian Efo Riro
imageAlt: Nigerian efo riro leafy vegetable stew
imageCredit: Image via Wikimedia Commons; see file page for author/license.
summary: Yoruba efo riro: leafy greens folded into a concentrated red-pepper and palm-oil sauce with fish and deeply savory seasoning.
lead: A pepper base cooks until its raw edge disappears before greens are folded in just long enough to become tender and glossy.
about: Efo riro is a Yoruba vegetable stew built from leafy greens and a pepper-tomato sauce enriched with palm oil and often fish, meat or both. The sauce should be concentrated before the greens enter so the finished dish is rich rather than watery.
story: Efo riro is common in Yoruba home cooking and celebration meals, paired with rice or swallows. Greens and proteins vary according to season and household.
caveat: This version uses spinach and smoked fish for accessibility; traditional greens and protein choices vary.
prepNotes: Raw watery sauce ruins the texture.
They should remain green and distinct.
Smoked fish can be very salty.
steps: Blend peppers, chile, half the onion and tomatoes coarsely.
Heat palm oil and cook remaining onion until soft.
Add pepper blend and simmer 15–20 minutes until reduced and oil shows at the edges.
Add crayfish and smoked fish and cook 5 minutes.
Fold in chopped greens.
Checkpoint: greens should be tender and glossy with no pool of thin red liquid.
Adjust seasoning and serve with rice or a swallow.
sources: Fringe Table — Maghreb & West Africa guide

name: Lowcountry Hoppin' John
imageCredit: Image via Wikimedia Commons; see file page for author/license.
summary: Lowcountry Hoppin' John with field peas, rice and smoked pork, rooted in African American and Gullah Geechee rice traditions.
lead: Field peas and rice cook together with smoked pork in a Lowcountry dish inseparable from African American food history.
about: Hoppin' John is a Lowcountry rice-and-pea dish traditionally associated with field peas or cowpeas, rice and smoked pork. It is especially linked to New Year's tables, though the dish belongs to a much broader Lowcountry food tradition.
story: Food historians connect Hoppin' John to West African rice and cowpea traditions preserved and transformed by enslaved Africans and their descendants in the Carolina Lowcountry. Modern versions using black-eyed peas are common, while Sea Island red peas more closely reflect older regional ingredients.
caveat: Sea Island red peas are ideal where available; black-eyed peas are a practical substitute.
ingredients: 1 1/2 cups cooked field peas or black-eyed peas
4 oz smoked bacon or ham hock
steps: Render bacon or brown ham hock in a pot.
Add onion and cook until soft.
Stir in rice for 1 minute.
Add peas, broth and thyme.
Cover and simmer 18 minutes without stirring.
Checkpoint: rice should be tender and separate with liquid fully absorbed.
Rest covered 10 minutes, fluff and season.
sources: Gullah Geechee Cultural Heritage Corridor — foodways

name: Armenian Spas
imageCredit: Image via Wikimedia Commons; see file page for author/license.
summary: Armenian spas: tangy yogurt soup with wheat berries, egg and herbs, served warm or cool depending on season.
lead: Yogurt becomes soup without curdling when it is tempered carefully with egg and wheat before gentle heating.
about: Spas is an Armenian yogurt-based soup commonly made with wheat berries or cracked wheat, egg and herbs such as cilantro or mint. The key technique is gradual heating so the yogurt remains smooth.
story: Spas appears across Armenian home cooking and may be served hot in cold weather or cool in summer. Grain and herb choices vary regionally.
caveat: Use full-fat plain yogurt for stability; lower-fat yogurt is more likely to split.
steps: Whisk yogurt, egg and flour until completely smooth.
Whisk in water gradually.
Place over medium-low heat and stir constantly until steaming and slightly thickened.
Add cooked wheat berries and salt; simmer very gently 10 minutes.
Sauté onion in butter until soft and add to soup.
Checkpoint: soup should be smooth and creamy with no curds.
Add herbs and serve warm or cooled.
sources: Fringe Table — Caucasus, Central & West Asia guide

name: Himachali Siddu
imageCredit: Image via Wikimedia Commons; see file page for author/license.
summary: Himachali siddu: yeast-raised wheat buns filled with walnuts and spices, then steamed until soft and served with ghee.
lead: A fermented wheat dough wraps a nutty filling and cooks in steam rather than an oven, producing a dense-soft mountain bread.
about: Siddu is associated with Himachal Pradesh and neighboring Himalayan areas. The wheat dough is fermented, filled and steamed; walnut, poppy-seed and lentil fillings are among documented variations.
story: Siddu reflects cool-climate Himalayan grain cookery and is often eaten hot with ghee or dal. Shape and filling differ across districts and households.
caveat: This version uses a walnut filling and a home steamer.
steps: Mix flour, yeast, salt and water into a soft dough; rise 60 minutes.
Grind walnuts, poppy seeds, scallions and cumin coarsely.
Divide dough into 8 pieces, flatten and fill.
Seal and rest 15 minutes.
Steam 18–22 minutes.
Checkpoint: buns should spring back lightly and show no raw dough at the center.
Brush with ghee and serve hot.
sources: Fringe Table — Himalayas & South Asia guide

name: Lao Mok Pa
imageAlt: Lao mok pa steamed fish in banana leaf
imageCredit: Image via Wikimedia Commons; see file page for author/license.
summary: Lao mok pa: fish mixed with lemongrass, dill and herbs, wrapped in banana leaf and steamed until fragrant and tender.
lead: Fish, herbs and aromatics steam inside banana leaf, trapping a distinctly Lao perfume of lemongrass, dill and chile.
about: Mok pa is a Lao steamed fish preparation in which seasoned fish is enclosed in banana leaf and gently cooked. Dill is especially characteristic, alongside lemongrass, makrut lime and other fresh aromatics.
story: Mok-style banana-leaf steaming is part of Lao cooking's emphasis on fresh herbs and gentle moist heat. Fish species and herb proportions change with river, season and household.
caveat: Foil-lined parchment can substitute for banana leaf for containment, but the aroma will differ.
steps: Warm banana leaves briefly over heat to soften.
Mix fish with lemongrass, dill, cilantro, scallion, lime leaf, chile, fish sauce and egg.
Divide mixture among leaf squares and fold into tight packets.
Arrange packets in a steamer.
Steam 20–25 minutes.
Checkpoint: fish should be opaque, flaky and at least 145°F in the center.
Open carefully and serve with sticky rice.
